newsitem.title: NORWAY: Credit-financed demand worries Norway cenbank head.
newsitem.headline: Credit-financed demand worries Norway cenbank head.

text.p: Central bank governor Kjell Storvik said on Monday he was worried that credit-financed demand was growing too strongly in Norway.
In an interview with Reuters, Storvik also said strong economic growth called for a tight 1997 budget.

"Most indicators suggest strong underlying growth in Norway's economy," he said. "The central bank's credit indicator displays a clear impression of strong growth in credit-financed demand and thus supports this main picture."
Storvik said an early warning was the credit indicator, a measure of household borrowing which displayed underlying growth of 8.9 percent in June compared to 7.9 percent in May.
"It should hence be given its appropriate weight in judging the economic development we are facing in this country," he said.

The central bank governor reiterated that he expected the country's strong economic growth to continue into 1997, with accelerating prices and costs. "In light of this development, there is a need for a tight fiscal stance in the 1997 budget," said Storvik.

In May, the government projected a budget surplus this year of about 25 billion crowns, thanks mainly to high oil prices. Daily Aftenposten, giving no source, last week said the surplus could be as high as 35 billion crowns given the high oil prices.
Norway, which pumps about three million barrels of crude per day, is the world's largest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia.

The central bank on June 20 forecast 3.25 percent 1996 real growth in mainland gross domestic product (GDP), falling to 2.25 percent in 1997, with private consumption growing 4.0 and 2.75 percent respectively.
Storvik said the draft 1997 state budget, due on October 4, was the country's main tool to stabilise the economy.

"It is increasingly important that the fiscal policy is implemented in such a way that a stable exchange rate can be maintained in order to contribute to a moderate growth in prices and costs," said Storvik.

In June Storvik said Norway's economic situation did not call for lower interest rates. Asked if a sufficiently tight budget could alter this view, he said "I can see that it is an interesting question, but I would rather not speculate on future interest rates."
